newsitem.title: USA: Dollar rallies on German weakness, Yeltsin illness.
newsitem.headline: Dollar rallies on German weakness, Yeltsin illness.

text.p: The dollar rallied sharply Wednesday on gloomy economic forecasts in Germany and news that Russian President Boris Yeltsin had been hospitalized.
The greenback posted a two-year high against the German mark and a 30-month peak against the Swiss franc as investors unloaded European currencies in favour of the more stable U.S. unit.
"The dollar is extremely well bid. This thing with Yeltsin has people getting out of Germany," said Jay Wertheimer, senior currency trader at Banco di Sicilia in New York.
A Kremlin statement late in the trading session disclosed that Yeltsin, who had quintuple bypass surgery in November, had contracted pneumonia.

The specter of political instability in former Communist Russia sparked mark selling. Germany is Russia's largest trading partner and its economy could suffer if Yeltsin were replaced with a less-friendly leader.
The dollar rose as high as 1.5787 marks, its highest since January 1995, before ending at 1.5740, up from 1.5642 late Tuesday. The U.S. unit also rose to 1.3635 Swiss francs from 1.3535.
Asian and European markets had already pushed the dollar higher early in the session amid broad expectations that a report due Thursday would show record unemployment in Germany.
Also on Thursday, Germany's central bank, the Bundesbank, will conduct its regular fortnightly council meeting, which some analysts speculated might produce a cut in official German interest rates.
Lower German rates would boost the dollar by enhancing the relative value of assets priced in dollars.
"There may be some opportunity for the dollar to score further gains if we get a particularly bad employment report out of Germany," said Lisa Finstrom, currency analyst at Smith Barney.
Weakness in Europe, as well as Japan, contrasts starkly with the U.S. economy, which is growing steadily and attracting the lion's share of investment flows.
Despite a sharp decline in U.S. stock prices Wednesday, traders predicted the market would soon resume its recent trend toward record highs, bolstering the dollar.
"There's still a very positive feeling about U.S. assets and the dollar," Wertheimer said.

Against the yen, the dollar rebounded after two days of heavy selling. Traders noted Japanese officials fell silent after several had made comments earlier this week calling for a halt to the dollar's recent rally.
"The fact that we did not get another round of verbal intervention from the Japanese may have given speculators a little leeway to test the (yen's) downside," Finstrom said.
The dollar ended higher at 115.76 yen versus 115.25 late Tuesday.
In other trade, the dollar fell to Canadian $1.3518 from C$1.3560 as the Bank of Canada was forced to enter the market to sell the Canadian currency, which has rallied sharply in recent sessions.
The British pound fell to $1.6873 from $1.6948.
